steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing a meta-learning (MAML-based) approach for personalizing deep recommender models in production. Cover the limits of existing personalization approaches, the method, and a roadmap of the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Deep recommender models at large internet companies and the need for personalization
- Existing approaches: architectures vs. embeddings, and their limits
- Personalization depends on the objective / task definition
- Meta learning and MAML in recommendation
- Our approach (LiMAML) and results
- Paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Context
  - neural recommendation models popular at large internet companies
  - objectives: click-through rate (CTR), invite, visit prediction
  - diverse, evolving needs of millions of members; refreshed recommendations every day
- Existing approaches
  - set 1: architectural improvements for sophisticated feature interactions
    - deeper models, factorization-machine based, SOTA on several tasks
    - still global models across members/entities/items -> limited personalization
  - set 2: embeddings for sparse categorical features per user / entity (advertiser, job, industry segment)
    - some personalization
    - reliable only with lots of data per user -> frequent members only; data inefficient
- Personalization varies by application
  - ad CTR: per advertiser ID
  - user-item CTR: per user
  - job apply: per-user + job-to-industry segment
  - meta learning: different task definitions per use case
- Meta learning
  - learn new task fast from few samples, model learnt on many tasks
  - MAML: model-agnostic, changes optimization, works for any gradient-descent model
  - recent use for cold start CTR
  - meta learn ID embeddings for cold start items, or last few MLP layers from few interactions
- Our approach
  - general architecture; MAML to meta learn part of network per task (members, entities, both)
  - rest shared, same as existing architecture
  - original MAML nearly infeasible online at scale
  - meta-learnt sub-network output -> meta embeddings -> regular features at serving; hundreds of billions of parameters
  - frequent meta-finetuning keeps models fresh
  - LiMAML beats baselines across LinkedIn use cases
  - business impact + uplift for infrequent members
- Organization: Sec 2 related work, 3 preliminaries, 4 method, 5 productionization, 6 offline, 7 online A/B

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Since deep learning came along, recommendation models based on neural networks have become very popular at large internet companies for modeling many objectives, for example click-through rate (CTR) prediction, invite prediction and visit prediction. These models need to understand the individual needs of millions of members, which are diverse and keep evolving, and they need to give refreshed item recommendations every day.

Many approaches have been proposed to improve how these networks perform so that personalization is better. The first set of approaches proposes architectural improvements so the model learns sophisticated feature interactions. Deeper models with intricate architectures based on factorization machines got state of the art performance on several recommender system prediction tasks. But they are still global models that are served across all members, entities and items, and they have limited personalization. The second set of approaches uses embeddings to handle sparse categorical feature inputs per user or per entity (e.g. per advertiser, per job, per industry segment, etc.). These embedding based approaches give some personalization for each user or entity. However they can only learn reliable embeddings if there is a lot of data per user, so the personalization is limited to frequent members on the platform. So these models are data inefficient during learning.

The definition of personalization is different for different objectives and applications. For example, in an ad Click Through Rate (CTR) prediction task we may want personalized models for each advertiser ID. In a general user-item CTR prediction task we may want personalized models per user. And for a model that predicts if a user would apply for a job, personalization at a per-user and job-to-industry segment level might make more sense. In the meta learning framework this means designing different task definitions for different use cases.

- Meta learning
  - learn new task fast from few samples, using model learnt on many tasks
  - MAML: model-agnostic, changes optimization, works for any gradient-descent model
  - recent use in recsys for cold start CTR
  - meta learn ID embeddings for cold start items, or last few MLP layers from few interactions
- Our approach
  - MAML to meta learn part of network per task (members, entities, both); rest shared
  - original MAML nearly infeasible online at scale
  - meta embeddings as regular features at serving; hundreds of billions of parameters
  - frequent meta-finetuning keeps models fresh
  - LiMAML beats baselines across LinkedIn use cases; uplift for infrequent members
- Organization: Sec 2 related work, 3 preliminaries, 4 method, 5 productionization, 6 offline, 7 online A/B

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Since deep learning came along, recommendation models based on neural networks have become very popular at large internet companies for modeling many objectives, for example click-through rate (CTR) prediction, invite prediction and visit prediction. These models need to understand the individual needs of millions of members, which are diverse and keep evolving, and they need to give refreshed item recommendations every day.

Many approaches have been proposed to improve how these networks perform so that personalization is better. The first set of approaches proposes architectural improvements so the model learns sophisticated feature interactions. Deeper models with intricate architectures based on factorization machines got state of the art performance on several recommender system prediction tasks. But they are still global models that are served across all members, entities and items, and they have limited personalization. The second set of approaches uses embeddings to handle sparse categorical feature inputs per user or per entity (e.g. per advertiser, per job, per industry segment, etc.). These embedding based approaches give some personalization for each user or entity. However they can only learn reliable embeddings if there is a lot of data per user, so the personalization is limited to frequent members on the platform. So these models are data inefficient during learning.

The definition of personalization is different for different objectives and applications. For example, in an ad Click Through Rate (CTR) prediction task we may want personalized models for each advertiser ID. In a general user-item CTR prediction task we may want personalized models per user. And for a model that predicts if a user would apply for a job, personalization at a per-user and job-to-industry segment level might make more sense. In the meta learning framework this means designing different task definitions for different use cases.

In meta learning the goal is to learn a new task quickly and effectively from a small number of data samples, using a model that was learnt on a large number of different tasks. Prior work proposes a model-agnostic meta-learning algorithm (MAML). MAML changes the optimization approach so that it can be applied directly to any deep learning model trained with a gradient descent procedure. MAML based approaches have only recently started to get popular in recommendation systems, for handling cold start scenarios of CTR prediction models. They try to learn personalized user preferences by meta learning ID embedding vectors for cold start items, or by meta learning the final few layers of the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) from a few user interaction samples.

In this paper we extend all of these ideas and give a general architecture for personalizing deep recommender models with meta learning. We use MAML to meta learn a part of the network at a per-task level, and tasks can be members, entities or a combination of both. The rest of the network is shared across all tasks and is the same as the architecture for that application. The original MAML is nearly infeasible to productionize online in large scale recommendation systems. Our approach instead gives an easy way to deploy personalized models with hundreds of billions of parameters in production. We do this by converting the output of the meta-learnt sub-network into meta embeddings, and these embeddings are given as regular features when serving the deployed neural network. We also do meta-finetuning frequently, which keeps the models refreshed and personalized to the most recent user interactions on the platform. We show across several real-world use cases at LinkedIn that the proposed approach (we call it LiMAML) beats the baseline models in all use cases. Besides business impact, we look in depth at how this approach really uplifts model performance even for infrequent members with limited data. This makes a compelling case for adopting a meta learnt personalization strategy for all recommender system models.

Section 2 covers related work and Section 3 gives preliminaries on meta learning. Section 4 introduces our proposed methodology, and Section 5 shares some insights about LiMAML productionization. Sections 6 and 7 present offline experiments and online A/B testing results.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
With the advent of deep learning, neural-network based recommendation models have become very popular at large internet companies for modeling a variety of objectives, including click-through rate (CTR) prediction, invite prediction, and visit prediction. These models need to understand the diverse and evolving individual needs of millions of members and provide refreshed item recommendations every day.

An array of approaches have been proposed to improve the performance of such networks for better personalization. The first set of approaches propose architectural improvements to learn sophisticated feature interactions [1,2,3]. Deeper models with intricate architectures based on factorization machines have achieved state of the art performance on several recommender system prediction tasks. However, they remain global models served across all members, entities and items, with limited personalization. The second set of approaches leverage embeddings to handle sparse categorical feature inputs per user or per entity (e.g. per advertiser, per job, per industry segment, etc.) [4,5,6]. Embedding based approaches provide some degree of personalization for each user or entity, but they can only learn reliable embeddings when there is a significant amount of data per user, which limits their personalization scope to frequent members on the platform. In other words, such models are data inefficient during learning.

The definition of personalization generally varies across objectives and applications. For an ad Click Through Rate (CTR) prediction task, for example, we may want to build personalized models for each advertiser ID. For a general user-item CTR prediction task, we may want personalized models per user. For a model that predicts whether a user would apply for a job, a per-user and job-to-industry segment level personalization might make more sense. In the meta learning framework, this entails designing different task definitions for different use cases.

With meta learning, the goal is to quickly and effectively learn a new task from a small number of data samples using a model learnt on a large number of different tasks. [7] proposes a model-agnostic meta-learning algorithm (MAML) that modifies the optimization approach so that it can be directly applied to any deep learning model trained with a gradient descent procedure. Only recently have MAML based approaches started gaining popularity in recommendation systems for handling cold start scenarios of CTR prediction models [8,9,10]. These approaches learn personalized user preferences by meta learning ID embedding vectors for cold start items or by meta learning the final few layers of the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) based on few user interaction samples.

In this paper, we extend these ideas to provide a general architecture for personalizing deep recommender models via meta learning. We leverage MAML [7] to meta learn a part of the network at a per-task level, where tasks could be members or entities or a combination of both. The rest of the network is shared across all tasks and kept identical to the architecture for that application. Whereas the original MAML is nearly infeasible to productionize online in large scale recommendation systems, our approach provides an easy way to deploy personalized models with hundreds of billions of parameters in production, by converting the output of the meta-learnt sub-network into meta embeddings and providing these embeddings as regular features while serving the deployed neural network. By doing meta-finetuning frequently, we keep the models refreshed and personalized to the most recent user interactions on the platform. We demonstrate across several real-world use cases at LinkedIn that the proposed approach (termed LiMAML) beats the baseline models across all use cases. Along with business impact, we dive deep into how this approach uplifts model performance even for infrequent members with limited data, presenting a compelling case for adopting a meta learnt personalization strategy for all recommender system models.

We go over related work in Section 2 and provide preliminaries on meta learning in Section 3. Section 4 introduces our proposed methodology, and Section 5 shares insights around LiMAML productionization. Offline experiments and online A/B testing results are presented in Sections 6 and 7 respectively.
